Meaning: Vigilant awareness of Allah that produces reverence, obedience, and restraint from sin. It includes the sense of protecting oneself from divine displeasure, so neither "fear" nor "piety" alone is sufficient.

Affirming Allah's absolute oneness and directing every act of worship to Him alone. It is more than belief in one deity; it also governs devotion, obedience, and one's understanding of divine lordship and attributes.
Faith involving inward conviction, verbal affirmation, and obedient commitment. In sermon language, it is a lived faith that can strengthen or weaken.
Willing submission to Allah through faith, worship, and obedience. The word describes both the religion of Islam and the act of surrendering to divine guidance.
Spiritual and moral excellence, especially worshipping Allah with deep awareness and treating creation well. It is broader than ordinary kindness.
Assigning to another what belongs exclusively to Allah, especially worship or divine authority. It includes obvious and subtle forms, not only belief in several gods.
Purifying worship and intention from all rivals and self-display. It is exclusive devotion to Allah, not frankness alone.
The heart's purposeful resolve that identifies and directs an act. It distinguishes acts and makes ordinary conduct devotional.
The divinely ordained way of faith, worship, ethics, and accountability. Depending on context, the same word can also mean judgment or recompense.
The original God-given human disposition that is receptive to truth and worship. It is not every natural impulse or acquired social habit.
Loving and humble obedience to Allah through all inward and outward acts He approves. It includes belief, intention, ethics, and daily conduct as well as formal rituals.

The human condition of devoted servitude and complete dependence on Allah. Although the literal root relates to servitude, the theological sense is honourable worshipful belonging, not human enslavement.
Reverent humility and attentive stillness of the heart and body before Allah, especially in prayer. It combines inward presence, submission, and outward composure.
Reliance of the heart on Allah while using lawful and effective means. It rejects both passive fatalism and treating worldly causes as independently sufficient.
Steadfast self-restraint in obeying Allah, avoiding sin, and enduring hardship. It is active perseverance rather than passive waiting.
Recognizing a blessing as coming from its giver, praising the giver, and using the blessing rightly. Gratitude is expressed through the heart, speech, and action.
A sincere return from sin to obedience through regret, stopping the offence, and resolving not to repeat it. It is a change of direction, not an apology alone.
Seeking Allah's forgiveness and protection from the blame and consequences of sin. It can accompany repentance but is not limited to saying a formula.
Remembering or mentioning Allah, receiving a reminder, or the revealed reminder itself. Context can refer to devotional remembrance, the Qur'an, or moral recollection.
Calling upon Allah through request, praise, or worship. It usually means supplication and is distinct from the formal ritual prayer.
Compassionate care that brings benefit and removes harm. When attributed to Allah, it refers to mercy bestowed in a manner fitting His majesty, not human weakness or indulgence.
Allah's covering and forgiving of sin while protecting the person from its harm. The concept includes pardon and safeguarding, not simply overlooking wrongdoing.
Pardon that removes blame and may erase the trace or consequence of an offence. It can convey more complete effacement than forgiveness alone.
Guidance that shows the right path and, when granted by Allah, can also enable a person to follow it. Context distinguishes explanation from inward direction and success.
Losing or departing from the path of right guidance. It can range from confusion to culpable rejection and is stronger than an ordinary mistake.
A context-dependent term for a test, temptation, persecution, destabilizing trial, punishment, or civil strife. Its central image is a process that exposes or tests what is genuine.
A test permitted or decreed by Allah that reveals a person's response and may refine character. It can occur through hardship or prosperity, not only calamity.
Settled certainty free of destabilizing doubt. In spiritual discourse it has degrees and transforms conduct, not only intellectual confidence.
The unseen realm inaccessible to ordinary direct perception. It includes realities known through revelation, not simply what humans have not discovered yet.
Allah's measured decree and apportionment of creation and events. Unlike blind fate, it is connected with divine knowledge, will, measure, and creation.
A decisive judgment, completion, or enactment. In theology it can refer to Allah's decree taking effect; in law it can mean judicial judgment, so context is essential.
Divine will by which events occur or do not occur. It is an effective will, not an uncertain wish.
Contented acceptance of Allah's decree without inward rebellion. It does not prevent grief, treatment, or lawful efforts to change a difficult situation.
Hope in Allah's mercy accompanied by pursuit of the actions that lead to it. Hope without repentance or effort can become mere wishful thinking.
Fear of Allah and accountability that restrains wrongdoing and encourages obedience. Its purpose is moral vigilance, not paralysis or panic.
Reverent fear arising from knowledge of Allah's greatness and one's responsibility before Him. It carries a stronger sense of awe and recognition than ordinary fear.
Steadfast uprightness upon faith without deviating to extremes. It is comprehensive consistency in creed, worship, and conduct.
Firmness upon truth, especially under trial. It is steadfast constancy, not immobility.
Serenity and stabilizing assurance bestowed by Allah, especially during fear or upheaval. It is an inward settling of the heart rather than ordinary quiet.
Deep settled tranquility arising from faith and remembrance. It is inward rest and confidence, not absence of difficulty.
Enduring and fruitful good placed by Allah in a person, action, time, or possession. It is not luck and may appear as increase, benefit, or lasting value.
Whatever provision Allah apportions, including material resources, health, knowledge, opportunity, and spiritual benefit. It is broader than salary or income.
What is religiously lawful and released from prohibition. It is a legal-moral category, not merely food certification.
What Allah has decisively prohibited. It is a binding legal category, not a cultural dislike.
A resemblance or uncertainty that makes falsehood appear plausible or a ruling appear doubtful. It can refer to intellectual confusion or an ambiguous matter.
Scrupulous restraint from doubtful or spiritually harmful matters. It is cautious moral self-protection beyond bare legality.
The Prophet's normative teaching, practice, and approved way; in other contexts, an established practice or recurring divine pattern. The intended sense must be determined from context.
A practice introduced into religion as worship without a valid basis. In this sermon context, it does not refer to every new tool, technology, or ordinary custom.
Deep understanding of religion and its practical implications. In technical usage, it especially refers to knowledge of Islamic legal rulings and their reasoning.
A qualified scholar's nonbinding legal answer to a religious question. It differs from a court judgment, which can be legally enforceable.
The divinely revealed path encompassing faith, worship, ethics, and law. Reducing it to criminal penalties or court rules seriously narrows the concept.
Disciplined reasoning by a qualified scholar to derive or apply a religious ruling. It is not unrestricted personal opinion.
Following a qualified juristic authority without independently deriving the proof. It is technical reliance, not necessarily mindless copying.
An indication or proof that guides to a conclusion. It may denote a recognized source or specific proof.
A decisive proof that establishes truth and responsibility. It denotes evidence that leaves no valid excuse, not rhetorical debate.
Clear demonstrative proof that decisively establishes a claim. It is stronger than a supporting reason; it implies manifest evidence.
Divine communication conveyed to a prophet in the manner Allah chooses. It is authoritative revelation, not private intuition or creative inspiration.
Allah's recited revelation given to Prophet Muhammad, whose wording and recitation are themselves sacred. It is a proper name, not simply "a reading.".
A sign that points beyond itself; depending on context, a verse of the Qur'an, a miracle, or a sign in creation.
Disciplined explanation of revelation using language, context, transmitted reports, and principles. It is a scholarly method, not personal paraphrase.
A contextually justified interpretation, final outcome, or ultimate realization of a text or event. Classical usage is broader than free allegorical interpretation.
Deep, consequence-aware reflection on revelation. The concept comes from considering what lies behind and follows a statement; it aims at guidance and action.
Right understanding joined to sound judgment and appropriate action. It can mean Prophetic teaching, revelation, or placing matters correctly.
A heart-directed admonition combining teaching, warning, encouragement, and compassionate counsel. Its aim is moral awakening, not information alone.
Sincere concern for another's good expressed through truthful, wise counsel. It conveys loyal moral sincerity, not criticism for its own sake.
Inviting people to Allah with knowledge, wisdom, and suitable means. It is principled invitation, not coercion or publicity alone.
Restoring what has become corrupt to soundness and right relation. It can be personal, familial, social, or political and is bounded by justice.
What revelation and sound custom recognize as right, fitting, and socially honourable. It is more than whatever is familiar.
What revelation and sound moral judgment recognize as wrong or unacceptable. It is not simply something unfamiliar.
Giving each person or matter its due and judging without bias or excess. Justice does not always require identical treatment when relevant circumstances differ.
Manifest fairness that gives each party its due. It stresses enacted and measurable justice, especially in dealings and testimony.
Violating a right or placing something outside its proper place, including wronging oneself through sin. It ranges from personal wrongdoing to systemic injustice.
Defiant departure from obedience and moral bounds. It suggests knowingly breaking out of rightful obedience, not generic badness.
Outwardly displaying faith while concealing unbelief, or behaving with traits associated with such duplicity. Sermons may use the word doctrinally or as a warning about hypocritical conduct.
Rejecting, denying, or covering over divine truth. The word has theological and legal uses, and applying it to particular people requires context and care.
Major sins marked by severe warning, punishment, curse, or prescribed penalty. It is juristic-theological, not based on social perception.
Performing worship or virtue to be seen and praised by people. Being visible is not itself showing off; the corrupting factor is the intention to gain admiration.
Arrogance expressed by rejecting truth and looking down on people. It is distinct from healthy dignity or confidence.
Resenting another's blessing and wishing for its removal. It is specifically hostile toward another's good; lawful emulation differs.
Mentioning a person's real fault in their absence in a way they would dislike. If the claim is false, it becomes slander rather than backbiting.
Carrying people's words between them to provoke conflict or damage relations. It is tale-bearing with corruptive effect, not all casual conversation.
A prohibited increase or exchange imbalance defined by Islamic commercial law. It includes many forms of interest but is a wider juristic category than the English word alone.
The obligatory, calculated share of qualifying wealth given to designated recipients. It is a legal right of recipients, not merely voluntary charity.
Giving for Allah's sake as an expression of sincere faith. It usually means voluntary charity, though some contexts also use it for obligatory zakat.
A trust or responsibility that must be faithfully protected and fulfilled. It includes entrusted property, duties, rights, and confidential information, not honesty alone.
A binding pledge, entrusted obligation, or covenant. It can denote divine covenant, human commitment, or a duty whose breach is betrayal.
A solemn binding covenant, often witnessed before Allah. It is stronger than a contract; it carries sacred and moral accountability.
Comprehensive righteousness expressed through faith, worship, generosity, and good character. It is broader than a single charitable act.
Maintaining kinship through contact, care, support, and reconciliation. The form varies with need and custom; it is broader than visits.
Comprehensive goodness, reverence, service, and gentle speech toward parents. It remains required within lawful limits even when parent and child disagree.
A community united by a shared faith, purpose, or messenger; in sermons, usually the worldwide Muslim community. It is not identical to a nation-state or ethnicity.
The united Muslim community or a body gathered around legitimate guidance. The word can also simply mean a group, so theological claims depend on context.
A bond of mutual loyalty, dignity, and responsibility grounded in faith or humanity. Ukhuwwah entails rights and duties, not emotional closeness alone.
The Islamic principle of consulting relevant people before making a responsible decision. It is not identical to a single modern political system or to majority voting in every matter.
The appointed end of earthly life and transition to the next stage of existence. In Islamic preaching, death is not annihilation but movement toward accountability.
The final and everlasting realm after worldly life, including resurrection, judgment, and recompense. It is the setting in which earthly choices reach their ultimate outcome.
The resurrection and great standing of creation before Allah for judgment. The word emphasizes rising and standing, not only the destruction of the world.
Allah's reckoning of beliefs, intentions, words, and deeds. It is moral accounting, not arithmetic alone.
The divinely just weighing of deeds, records, or people on the Day of Judgment. It expresses exact accountability and is treated in sermons as an eschatological reality.
The straight path of guidance, and in eschatological contexts the crossing over Hell toward Paradise. The intended meaning depends on the passage.
Intercession granted only by Allah's permission and approval. It is not an automatic spiritual privilege or a means of overriding divine judgment.
The divinely prepared everlasting abode of nearness, safety, and reward. It is Paradise; the root image of a concealed garden does not exhaust the concept.
The divinely created abode or punishment of the condemned. It means Hell, not every physical flame.
Comprehensive success: attaining lasting good and escaping ultimate harm. It is salvation-flourishing, not worldly achievement alone.
Ultimate and irrecoverable loss of oneself, one's deeds, or salvation. It is much broader than financial loss.
Allah's enabling a person to choose, pursue, and accomplish what is right. It joins sound intention, ability, and successful action.
Soundly directed judgment and conduct leading to a good end. It combines intellectual rightness, maturity, and practical direction.
Detachment of the heart from excessive attachment to worldly things in favour of the Hereafter. It does not require poverty or abandoning lawful possessions.
Contentment with what suffices, without greedy fixation on more. It is freedom from acquisitive restlessness, not lack of ambition.
Preferring another's legitimate need over one's own despite personal need. It is self-giving rooted in faith, not indiscriminate self-neglect.
Beautiful moral character in one's habitual dealings. It includes patience, justice, mercy, and restraint, not etiquette alone.
Humility that gives others their due without arrogance or self-abasement. It preserves dignity while rejecting claims of superiority.
Moral modesty and sensitivity that restrain shameful conduct. It is not social fear or an inability to speak confidently.
The Lord who creates, owns, sustains, governs, and nurtures creation. The word conveys comprehensive divine care and authority, not merely the social title "master.".
The being who is worshipped; in Islamic creed, Allah alone is rightfully worshipped. The concept concerns entitlement to worship, not power alone.
Exclusive divine right to worship. It is a creed term denoting that all worship belongs to Allah alone.
Allah's unique lordship over creation. It includes creating, owning, sustaining, decreeing, and governing all things.
A divine name expressing vast, all-encompassing mercy. Its intensive form conveys the abundance and breadth of Allah's mercy.
A divine name expressing continuing and specially bestowed mercy. It conveys enduring mercy rather than an ordinary kindly disposition.
The Oft-Forgiving who repeatedly covers and pardons sin. It stresses abundance and recurrence of forgiveness.
The Constantly and Abundantly Forgiving. It is stronger than a one-time act of pardon; it conveys repeated forgiveness.
The divine name of the One who pardons and effaces sin. It can imply removal of blame and its trace, beyond withholding punishment.
The One who repeatedly turns to servants in mercy and accepts repentance. It means enabling and accepting repentance, not repenting Himself.
The divine name expressing especially tender and gentle mercy that relieves suffering.
The Loving and Beloved, whose love is active and beneficent. It is not sentiment alone but favour, nearness, and benevolence.
The Subtly Kind and perfectly aware of hidden details. It combines subtle knowledge with unobtrusive kindness and providence.
The One fully acquainted with inner realities and outcomes. It is not merely possessing information; it implies penetrating knowledge of what is hidden.
The All-Knowing without limit or acquisition. It denotes complete, timeless, and unfailing knowledge.
The Perfectly Wise who places everything appropriately. It includes perfect judgment, purpose, and right placement, not cleverness alone.
The Forbearing who does not hasten punishment despite power. It is deliberate restraint, not inability or passivity.
The divine name expressing supreme generosity, nobility, honour, and graciousness.
The Most Generous and Most Noble. It carries both munificence and incomparable nobility.
The Unceasing Bestower of gifts without compensation. It stresses free, repeated, undeserved bestowal.
The Constant Provider who creates and delivers all provision. It includes material, spiritual, lawful, and inward sustenance.
The divine name meaning the Opener who grants relief, opens paths of mercy or victory, and judges decisively between parties. The intended emphasis depends on context.
The perfectly effective Helper who protects, supports, and grants victory.
The Protecting Patron and Ally who is near to His servants. The word can combine protection, authority, loyalty, and closeness, so "friend" is too weak.
The Patron, Master, Protector, or Ally. It is a relational term whose exact English rendering depends on who is speaking and the surrounding context.
The fully sufficient Trustee upon whom all affairs may be entrusted. In contexts of reliance on Allah, it means the One who manages matters perfectly.
The Perfect Preserver and Watchful Guardian. It includes guarding, preserving, recording, and preventing loss.
The Ever-Watchful Observer from whom nothing is absent. It conveys continuous, morally consequential oversight, not surveillance alone.
The One who is fully sufficient for His servants and who reckons all deeds exactly. Both meanings are used in religious language.
The ever-present Witness whose knowledge misses nothing. As a divine name, it does not mean a person killed as a martyr.
The Sustainer who apportions nourishment and preserves creation, with complete power over it. The word has a wider sense than "feeder.".
The One whose power and ability are complete and unrestricted. Divine power is fully effective, not merely potential.
The All-Powerful who determines and effects all things. It is an intensive divine attribute of comprehensive power.
The Supremely Powerful whose power is manifest and irresistible. It emphasizes exercised and overwhelming power.
The Perfectly Strong, untouched by weakness. It is absolute and not bodily.
The Firm and Unfailing in strength. It conveys unbreakable, inexhaustible power rather than physical hardness.
The Irresistible One whose authority cannot be overcome and who restores what is broken. As a divine name, it does not mean an unjust tyrant.
The Supremely Great, exalted above every defect and rival. Arrogant pride is blameworthy in creatures, whereas this divine name expresses rightful greatness and transcendence.
The Incomparably Great in essence, rank, and authority. It does not refer to physical size; it denotes absolute greatness.
The Tremendously Magnificent and worthy of awe. It carries a stronger sacred sense than the ordinary word "great.".
The Most High in rank, authority, and transcendence. It does not refer only to spatial height; it denotes exaltedness above all imperfection.
The Supremely Exalted above all limitation and false attribution. An intensive expression of transcendence.
The Absolutely Pure and Holy, exalted above every defect and creaturely limitation. "Holy" is only an approximate English equivalent.
The One free from every defect and the source of safety and peace. As a divine name, it means more than tranquillity.
The Giver of security and the One who confirms truth. As a divine name, it does not mean "a believer.".
The Supreme Overseer, Guardian, and Witness whose authority and knowledge encompass all things.
The One without partner in divinity. It is not merely numerical oneness; it denies any partner or division in worship and lordship.
The Uniquely One, indivisible and without equal. In creed, it expresses absolute uniqueness rather than numerical oneness alone.
The Self-Sufficient Master upon whom all creation depends. No single English word fully captures both perfect independence and universal dependence upon Him.
A firmly held conviction concerning matters of faith. The word comes from the idea of binding or tying, suggesting a settled belief rather than a casual opinion.
A divinely grounded religious way or confessional tradition. It denotes the inherited or followed way of faith, especially the creed of Abraham.
A binding responsibility, legal liability, or protected covenantal status. The exact sense can be obligation, protection, or guarantee depending on context.
Faithful allegiance, protective loyalty, and committed solidarity. Its theological and communal sense is stronger and more relational than preference.
Disavowal of false worship and principled separation from wrongdoing. It does not simply mean personal innocence.
Deliberate renunciation of Islam after professing it. A technical legal-theological term, not every doubt or sinful act.
Concealed heterodoxy or unbelief presented outwardly as Islam. Historically the label has been used in different ways and should not be treated as a precise name for every doctrinal error.
Deviation from truth, especially denial of God or distortion of His signs. Qur'anic and classical usage is broader than modern atheism.
Division into a distinct faction, often through doctrinal or communal rupture. It can mean mere group, separation, or blameworthy factionalism according to context.
Perverse misdirection chosen in opposition to sound guidance. It implies morally blameworthy deviation, not innocent confusion.
Anything worshipped, obeyed, or followed in rebellion against Allah's authority and limits. It can refer to a false deity, satanic authority, tyrannical power, or a claimant to divine rights.
A broad Qur'anic term for false objects of worship, superstition, sorcery, or other forms of religious falsehood. Its exact referent depends on context.
Rivals set up as equals or counterparts to Allah. It stresses treating created things as peers in love, obedience, or worship.
Intercessors whose mediation is sought or granted. Intercession in Islamic theology is dependent on Allah's permission, not independent influence.
Will or intention. In theology, divine will may refer either to what Allah commands and loves or to what He allows to occur in creation.
Bringing into existence according to measure; also the created order. It can denote the act of creating, created beings, or innate constitution.
Human acquisition of deeds and their moral responsibility. It describes accountable human action under divine creation and decree.
The capacity and means by which a person is able and accountable. It is a technical term in debates about responsibility, power, and action.
Being charged by divine law with accountable duties. It signifies morally binding religious responsibility, not merely a task.
Certainty reached through reliable knowledge, evidence, or report. It is the first of three Qur'anic expressions describing degrees or modes of certainty.
Certainty comparable to direct seeing. It describes immediate experiential confirmation, not a literal "eye" belonging to certainty.
Certainty fully realized through direct encounter with reality. It is the most complete expression in the Qur'anic sequence of certainty.
Testimony or witnessing; it can also mean the visible, perceptible realm. Context may refer to legal evidence, the confession of faith, martyrdom, or the world of direct perception.
Declaring Allah free of every defect and creaturely limitation. It is a theological act of transcendence, not praise in general.
Likening divine attributes to created qualities. It denotes anthropomorphic assimilation, not every analogy.
Denying, emptying, or suspending the meanings of divine attributes. A technical theological term, not ordinary interruption.
The sending down of revelation in stages and with divine authority. It highlights descent from Allah and often gradual delivery.
The divinely prescribed Scripture or authoritative written decree. It may mean the Quran, a prior scripture, a record, or a decree.
The divine criterion that separates truth from falsehood. It can name the Qur'an or any decisive divine distinction.
Guidance that directs toward truth and a sound end. It refers to revelation or divine enabling, not information alone.
Divine illumination that makes truth spiritually perceptible. It usually metaphorical and revelatory, not physical light.
Clear proofs or insights that illuminate spiritual and moral truth. The plural refers to inward perception and evidence, not physical eyesight.
Clear exposition that makes meaning distinct. In Qur'anic rhetoric it implies clarification and eloquent disclosure.
Comprehensive clarification and exposition. It is an intensive form suggesting fullness of clarification.
A distinct Qur'anic chapter of elevated, enclosed composition. It is a sacred textual unit, not merely a book chapter.
A text whose meaning or ruling is firmly established and relatively clear. In Qur'anic studies, definitions vary according to the way it is contrasted with mutashabih.
A text whose exact meaning, application, or ultimate referent is not immediately decisive. It may require interpretation or humble suspension of judgment and is not necessarily contradictory.
A later ruling or text that replaces the operative legal ruling of an earlier one. The concept concerns legal effect, not denial of the earlier revelation.
A ruling whose operative legal force has been replaced by a later ruling. The earlier verse or report remains part of revelation or transmission even when its ruling no longer applies.
Ordered recitation, especially of revelation, with an older root sense of following. It implies more than vocal reading and can suggest following what is recited.
Measured, clear, and deliberate recitation of the Qur'an. It emphasizes correct articulation, pacing, and reflection rather than musical performance.
Reciting the Qur'an while giving each letter and recitation rule its proper pronunciation. It concerns disciplined phonetic accuracy, not ornamentation alone.
The act of reading or reciting; in Qur'anic studies, a formally transmitted canonical mode of recitation.

In the expression "seven ahruf," a technical term for divinely permitted modes of early Qur'anic recitation. Scholars differ about their precise nature, but the word does not mean seven alphabet letters or the seven canonical readings.
The inherited consonantal spelling and written form of the Qur'anic codex. It is a technical term for orthography, not drawing.
A physical written codex containing the Qur'anic text. It is the written copy, whereas the Qur'an is the revealed recitation and message.
The chain through which a report or recitation is attributed to its source. It is a formal transmission chain, not "support" in the general sense.
A transmitted report, narration, or version received through a chain. In Qur'anic recitation, it can mean a formally transmitted recension associated with a reader.
Critical understanding of meaning, method, and content. It is often contrasted with mere transmission because it requires analytical comprehension.
Knowledge based on sound evidence and understanding. In religious sermons, it often refers to sacred or beneficial knowledge rather than modern science specifically.
A reminder that restores awareness of a truth already known or naturally recognizable. It carries the sense of moral recollection and warning.
Beneficial recollection or a reminder that awakens the heart. It usually refers to the effect of being reminded, not autobiographical memory.
A moral lesson drawn by moving from an event or sign to its deeper meaning. It is more than an example.
Reflective inference that draws a lesson from signs, history, or outcomes. It is not mere attention; it involves moral and analogical reasoning.
Inner clarity that perceives truth and guides action. It is spiritually and intellectually informed perception, not intuition alone.
Discernment that reads outward signs with trained inward perception. In ethical discourse, it is perceptiveness rather than fortune-telling or certainty about the unseen.
Accurate apprehension of intended meaning. In sacred learning it includes context, implication, and proper application.
Preservation in memory and faithful safeguarding. It can mean memorizing, protecting the text, or retaining knowledge through practice.
Careful verification before accepting or acting on information. It means checking truth and avoiding haste, especially regarding reports.
Seeking and attaining clarity through verification. In a command, it means to investigate carefully rather than merely notice.
Conscientious seeking of what is most correct and truthful. It includes moral scrupulousness and careful choice.
Issuing a reasoned religious legal answer to a particular question. It is nonjudicial guidance based on recognized legal method.
A qualified scholar authorized to issue legal responses. It requires juristic competence, not merely religious status.
Following guidance with awareness of its basis and direction. It is often praised as adherence to revelation, in contrast with blind imitation.
A transmitted report or remaining trace, often from early authorities. In hadith discourse it may refer to a report from a Companion or predecessor.
Authoritative transmission of text or report. It contrasts with pure reasoning and refers to transmitted evidence.
The faculty of understanding and moral restraint. Classical usage connects sound reasoning with the ability to restrain oneself from error.
Disciplined examination leading toward knowledge. In theology and legal theory it means reasoned consideration.
Reasoning from evidence to a warranted conclusion. A technical scholarly process, not rhetorical persuasion.
A strong appetite or desire that may draw a person beyond lawful limits. It includes desire for food, status, wealth, and sex, not sexual desire alone.
A person who sincerely affirms and confirms the truth. In faith contexts, the word suggests inward acceptance that leads to truthful response.
One who submits to Allah and enters the community of Islam. It is active surrender and obedience.
One who acts with excellence and worships with heightened awareness of Allah. It denotes sustained spiritual-moral excellence, not isolated kindness.
A person who protects themselves from Allah's displeasure through vigilant obedience and avoidance of sin. "Pious" is only a partial equivalent.
One who purifies intention and devotion exclusively for Allah. It carries exclusivity of worship, not honesty alone.
A person of exceptional truthfulness whose faith fully confirms divine truth. In sacred usage, it denotes a high spiritual rank, not an ordinary friend.
A God-oriented scholar and educator who combines knowledge, wisdom, and gradual spiritual formation of others.
One whose faith, character, and conduct are sound and reforming. It includes being rightly ordered and beneficial, not merely pleasant.
One who defiantly departs from obedience or moral bounds. It can be legal or moral; it should not be casually over-applied.
A person who violates rights or places worship, conduct, or judgment outside its proper place. The word includes wronging oneself and associating partners with Allah, not only political oppression.

A person who outwardly professes faith while concealing unbelief; sermon language may also warn about hypocritical traits. The doctrinal label should not be casually applied to particular individuals.

A person described in theology as rejecting or concealing divine truth. The legal and doctrinal label is context-sensitive and should not be used as a loose insult or automatic synonym for every non-Muslim.
A person who assigns a partner or rival to Allah in worship or divine rights. This includes devotional association, not only belief in many gods.
A person who deliberately renounces Islam after professing it. It is a technical legal status with conditions and is not established by mere doubt or sin.
A person who denies God or deviates from divine truth. Classical usage can be broader than the modern word "atheist.".
One who has lost or departed from right guidance. It may describe culpable deviation, confusion, or lack of guidance according to context.
A person heedless of Allah, accountability, or moral signs. The word describes spiritual unawareness, not ordinary absent-mindedness.
One whose heart is hardened against truth and compassion. It is inward resistance and insensitivity, not a firm personality.
One possessing settled certainty that shapes action. It implies embodied conviction, not merely confidence.
A person humbly settled, tranquil, and receptive before Allah. It combines lowliness, trust, and willing obedience.
A person inwardly humbled and outwardly composed before Allah. This describes reverent presence of heart expressed through bodily stillness.
One persistently obedient and devoutly standing before Allah. It may include prolonged worship, humble obedience, or supplication.
One who repeatedly returns to Allah in repentance and devotion. It suggests frequent, heartfelt returning, not a single apology.
One who turns back to Allah with reliance and obedient devotion. It is a sustained orientation toward Allah.
One who abandons sin, regrets it, and returns to obedience. It requires moral return, not verbal regret alone.
One who actively remembers and mentions Allah. It includes heart, tongue, awareness, and obedience.
One who recognizes blessings, praises the Giver, and uses blessings rightly. It is enacted gratitude, not emotion alone.
One who steadfastly restrains the soul upon obedience and through hardship. It means disciplined perseverance, not passive waiting.
One who relies upon Allah while taking legitimate means. It combines heart-reliance with responsible action.
One who hopes in Allah while pursuing the causes of mercy. It is morally active hope, not wishful thinking.
One who fears Allah in a way that restrains wrongdoing and motivates obedience. It is reverent moral fear, not panic.
A trembling inward awe awakened by awareness of Allah. It is a sensitive and reverent response rather than panic.
Awe-filled fear that turns a person away from wrongdoing. It is often paired with hopeful longing to express balanced worship.
Earnest longing directed toward Allah and His reward. In devotional contexts it is hopeful aspiration, not appetite.
Continual turning of the heart and conduct back to Allah. It is broader than repentance from a specific sin and describes an enduring devotional orientation.
Humble, tranquil submission and inward settling before Allah. The word evokes low, stable ground as an image of a settled heart.
Truthfulness and inner-outer congruence in word, intention, and covenant. It is a moral quality of being true, not factual accuracy alone.
Living with sustained awareness that Allah observes and knows all things. It is a spiritual practice of accountability, not surveillance of other people.
Examining and holding oneself accountable before final judgment. It means moral self-audit, not bookkeeping.
Disciplined striving against the ego, habits, and obstacles to obedience. In this context it commonly means inner moral struggle, not armed conflict.
Conscious recognition of one's complete need of Allah. It is spiritual and existential dependence, not merely financial poverty.
Spiritual nearness to Allah through His favour, worship, and obedience. It does not imply physical distance or bodily location.
Devotional love that entails preference, obedience, and longing. It is covenantal and transformative, not sentiment alone.
Spiritual yearning to meet Allah and attain His pleasure. It is an elevated devotional desire.
Intimate spiritual ease and comfort found in remembering and worshipping Allah. It is inward familiarity with devotion, not sociability.
A prescribed act of devotion, especially sacrificial or pilgrimage worship. It can denote worship generally or a specific sacrificial rite.
A divinely appointed symbol or rite that publicly marks devotion. It is a sacred sign whose honour reflects reverence for Allah.
The divinely established rites and symbols of worship. It carries sacred legal significance, not cultural pageantry.
The prescribed ritual prayer combining recitation, standing, bowing, and prostration. It is distinct from supplication.
Standing in worship, especially prolonged night prayer. It means devotional standing before Allah.
Ritual bowing that embodies humble submission. It is a prescribed prayer posture with devotional meaning.
Placing the forehead in prostration as the highest bodily act of worship. It denotes worshipful abasement to Allah, not ordinary bowing.
Prolonged devout obedience, standing, or supplication. Its exact meaning varies between Qur'anic passages and legal discussions.
The odd-numbered night prayer concluding voluntary worship. A technical devotional term, not arithmetic alone.
Voluntary night prayer performed after sleeping. It is often distinguished from voluntary prayer offered earlier in the night.
Ramadan night prayers performed with intervals of rest. The name reflects pauses between units, not relaxation as the purpose.
Recommended Prophetic practices or established normative ways. In other contexts, the plural can also refer to recurring patterns or laws established by Allah.
A voluntary act of worship beyond what is obligatory. It is spiritually meritorious and can repair deficiencies in obligatory worship.
Freely undertaken obedience beyond binding duty. It means optional devotion, not civic service.
A specifically apportioned and binding religious obligation. It is legally mandatory and divinely assigned.
A legally binding act whose omission is sinful. Some legal schools distinguish technically between this category and the closely related category of fard, while others use them nearly synonymously.
An integral element without which an act of worship is invalid. It is an internal essential component, not merely something important.
A prerequisite required before an act or ruling can be valid. A legal condition lies outside the act itself but determines validity.
Binding components or duties whose omission has legal consequence. The exact consequence differs across legal schools and acts.
Acts that invalidate worship or a legal transaction. These are technically defined nullifiers, not anything disliked.
An act religiously discouraged but not normally forbidden. The English word "hated" is too emotional for this technical legal category.
An act that is legally permitted in itself, without inherent reward or sin. Intention and consequences can change its moral value.
A matter whose lawful or unlawful status is not sufficiently clear. It calls for verification and caution, not suspicion toward people.
Ritual and physical purification required or encouraged for worship. It includes legal states not visible as dirt.
Ritual impurity defined by Islamic law. It is a juridical category, not general uncleanliness.
A state of minor or major ritual impurity that prevents certain acts of worship until purification. In Islamic law, it does not mean an ordinary event.
The prescribed washing and wiping before prayer. It is a specific ritual act with intention and ordered components.
The full ritual bath required in defined circumstances. It is a legal purification, not an ordinary shower.
Ritual purification with clean earth or dust when water is unavailable or cannot safely be used. It is a legally defined substitute, not ordinary "dry washing.".
Cleansing oneself after relieving oneself. It is a technical practice of ritual cleanliness, not general bathing.
Cleansing after relieving oneself with suitable dry material. Stones were historically common, but equivalent clean materials may fulfil the function.
Ritual wiping over a body part or permitted covering. It has precise conditions and is not interchangeable with washing.
The direction of the Kaaba faced during prayer. Without vowel marks, the word can be confused with a homograph meaning "kiss.".
Attentive awareness of Allah and the act of worship within the heart. It describes inward presence rather than concentration alone.
Declaring "Allah is greater" as an act of glorification, especially by saying "Allahu akbar.".
Praising Allah, especially by saying "al-hamdu lillah." The term often names this established formula of praise.
Declaring Allah free from every defect and limitation. It is more specific than general praise.
Saying "there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah." The term names this declaration of divine oneness, not chanting in general.
Saying "there is no power or ability except through Allah." The formula acknowledges that all effective strength and change depend on Him.
Saying "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs," or a related formula of reliance. The word is a devotional abbreviation, not calculation.
Seeking Allah's protection from evil. It is a worshipful appeal, commonly before recitation.
Saying "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful." The word is the technical name for beginning with this formula.
Saying "All praise belongs to Allah." The word is a coined name for this formula, not praise in general.
Asking Allah to bless, honour, and exalt Prophet Muhammad. The supplication is directed to Allah, not to the Prophet.
The formal public call announcing the time of prescribed prayer. It is a regulated act of worship with fixed wording.
The shorter call immediately preceding congregational prayer. The same Arabic form has unrelated everyday meanings.
Leadership of congregational prayer; more broadly, leadership, authority, or exemplary guidance. The intended meaning can differ significantly across legal, political, and theological contexts.
Following the prayer leader's actions in proper sequence. In congregational prayer it is a technical relationship to the imam.
Joining and following an imam in congregational prayer. It is a technical prayer term governing how the follower coordinates with the imam.
The aligned row of worshippers in congregational prayer. It carries ritual requirements of straightness and cohesion.
The weekly Friday congregational prayer and, by extension, its day. In religious context, it often refers to the institution of Friday worship rather than the weekday alone.
The formal sermon delivered as part of Friday or Eid worship. It has ritual and legal features beyond ordinary public speaking.
The pulpit from which the sermon is delivered. It carries Prophetic and communal symbolism in Islamic discourse.
Devotional seclusion in a mosque with intention of worship. It is a regulated religious practice, not a wellness retreat.
Worshipful abstention from defined things from dawn to sunset with intention. It includes spiritual restraint and legal conditions, not merely not eating.
Ending a fast at its lawful time; also not fasting when permitted. The common English sense can obscure the religious act.
The pre-dawn meal eaten before a day of fasting. It is a recommended Prophetic practice, not simply a late-night meal.
The major pilgrimage to Mecca performed through prescribed rites at a set time. It is a specific obligation, not any sacred journey.
The lesser pilgrimage consisting of entering consecration, circumambulating the Kaaba, and walking between Safa and Marwah. It is a defined act of worship, not simply visiting Mecca.
Entering the consecrated state for Hajj or Umrah through intention and prescribed restrictions. The familiar garments mark this state but are not the state itself.
Ritual circumambulation of the Kaaba in prescribed form. It is worship directed to Allah, not worship of the building.
The ritual walking between Safa and Marwah during Hajj or Umrah. Outside pilgrimage, the same word commonly means effort or striving.
Being present at Arafah during the prescribed pilgrimage time, an essential rite of Hajj. Continuous physical standing is not required.
Casting pebbles at the designated pillars during Hajj. The targets symbolize rejection of temptation; they are not literally Satan.
An animal offering designated for Hajj or Umrah. Without vowel marks, the word can be confused with another word meaning guidance.
The sacrificial animal offered during Eid al-Adha according to prescribed rules. It is a devotional offering, not a "victim.".
The animal sacrifice offered in gratitude for a newborn, commonly accompanied by naming and other practices. The term is not simply hair cutting.
Completely sincere and reforming, especially in the expression "sincere repentance." It describes repentance free of deception and accompanied by genuine correction.
Heartfelt remorse for having disobeyed Allah. It is morally focused regret and is described as the core of repentance.
Immediate cessation and abandonment of a sin. In repentance language it means stopping the offence, not gradual reduction.
Firm resolve of the heart to obey or not return to sin. It is a settled moral decision, not momentary motivation.
Graciously turning away from an offence without reproach. It suggests opening a new page rather than repeatedly mentioning the wrong.
Expiation or removal of sins; in another context, declaring a person to be an unbeliever. The surrounding words are essential because the two meanings are very different.
A prescribed act of expiation for a specific violation. It does not necessarily replace repentance, compensation, or restoration of another person's rights.
Righteous deeds and moral goods rewarded by Allah. It includes acts, qualities, and their reward-bearing effects.
Sins, evil deeds, or harmful consequences. It can denote offences themselves or the harms they produce.
Erasure or removal, especially Allah's erasing sins or their recorded effects. It is a theological image of complete removal, not computer deletion.
Allah's replacing evil deeds with good for sincere repenters. It is transformative, not mere relabelling.
Returning to Allah, truth, or obedience after departure. It describes existential return, not movement.
Frequent and loving return to Allah. It conveys repeated devotional return, stronger than ordinary coming back.
Seeking protection through prescribed remembrance, Qur'anic recitation, and supplication. It does not mean creating a magical shield.
Established formulas and acts of remembering Allah for recurring times and situations. They include praise, supplication, and Qur'anic phrases.
The pilgrimage response beginning "Labbayka," expressing readiness, obedience, and repeated response to Allah's call.
Affirming Allah's absolute sacredness and freedom from every imperfection. It concerns divine transcendence, not making something holy by human action.
Earnest, humble supplication made with deep need. It combines humility, intensity, and turning to Allah.
Praising Allah by mentioning His beautiful qualities and acts. It is reverent praise and is broader than repeating a single formula.
Seeking urgent rescue or relief. In theological discussion, the meaning and ruling depend on whom help is sought from and what ability is attributed to them.
Seeking help while recognizing that all ultimate power belongs to Allah. It may refer to ordinary assistance from people or devotional reliance on Allah.
Seeking reinforcement, support, or aid. Because the word can be used materially or spiritually, the source and kind of help must be clear from context.
A request or question. In devotional context, it can mean asking Allah for a need; in scholarly context, it means an issue under discussion.
Intimate, private conversation and supplication directed to Allah. It conveys closeness, confidentiality, and inward address.
Humble submission and loweredness before Allah, especially during hardship. It is voluntary spiritual yielding, not degradation before people.
Humble, broken-hearted pleading before Allah. It denotes spiritually truthful need, not degrading performance.
Contrite humility and awareness of need before Allah. It is not psychological collapse or loss of human dignity.
Affectionate love expressed through loyalty, care, and good treatment. It emphasizes warm, enacted affection rather than emotion alone.
Hopeful desire directed toward Allah. It is often paired with awe-filled fear to express balance between hope and fear.
Awe-filled fear that turns a person away from disobedience. It is devotional reverence, not panic.
A response to a call or supplication. Allah's answer to prayer may take a form other than the exact result requested.
Allah's gracious acceptance of worship or repentance. An act may be outwardly valid while its ultimate acceptance remains dependent on sincerity, conformity, and divine grace.
Granting or responding to a request. In the context of supplication, an answer does not necessarily mean immediate fulfilment in the exact form expected.
Persistent and repeated supplication without despair. It is praised when joined with humility, trust, and patience rather than entitlement.
Spiritual wakefulness after heedlessness. It is the heart's awakening to mortality, sin, and divine signs.
Heedless absence from awareness of Allah and the Hereafter. A person may remember facts yet remain spiritually heedless.
Forgetting; sometimes neglecting or abandoning what one was commanded to remember. It may carry moral neglect, not involuntary forgetting only.
Deliberate reflection on signs, creation, and meaning. It is worshipful reasoning aimed at recognition and reform.
Recovering and responding to a truth through reminder. It includes moral receptivity, not recall alone.
Bringing a meaning consciously before the heart. It means sustaining awareness of divine presence and intention.
Entrusting the result of one's affairs to Allah after responsible effort. It is inward surrender, not abandonment of action.
Settled confidence in Allah's promise, wisdom, and care. The word itself can mean trust generally, so its object must be clear.
Expecting Allah's mercy, wisdom, and good treatment while continuing repentance and obedience. It is not presumption that actions have no consequences.
Unfounded negative suspicion about Allah or other people. It can concern divine wisdom, another person's motives, or social conduct and must be understood from context.
Impatiently demanding an answer or outcome before its wise time. In supplication, it includes losing hope because the request was not answered quickly.
Despairing of Allah's mercy. It is a theological-moral loss of hope, not ordinary discouragement.
Loss of hope, especially in relief or mercy. It can become blameworthy when it denies Allah's power or compassion.
Glad tidings that announce divine favour or a hopeful outcome. It carries authoritative promise and spiritual encouragement.
A warning given before accountability so that danger can be avoided. In prophetic speech, it is advance moral warning rather than mere intimidation.
Rejoicing in received or promised divine favour. It conveys inward gladness awakened by good news.
Divinely granted opening and relief after constriction. It denotes unexpected release from hardship.
Severe constriction, anguish, and overwhelming distress. It is stronger than ordinary pressure or stress.
Private conversation or secret counsel. Qur'anic usage can refer positively to intimate supplication or negatively to concealed plotting.
A legitimate means of drawing nearer to Allah. The term names the means itself and does not automatically specify a disputed form of intercession.
Seeking nearness to Allah or an answer to prayer through a recognized means. Jurists differ about some forms, so the specific means must be identified.
Invoking or affirming Allah's blessing for a person or thing. It is a prayer that Allah place enduring good, not a transfer of mystical energy.
Fair-minded recognition of another person's right, even against oneself. It implies surrendering personal advantage when truth requires it.
Abundant dutiful goodness, especially toward parents and those with rights. It includes tenderness and service, not mechanical compliance.
Maintaining active bonds of kinship through contact, care, support, and reconciliation. In sermon usage, the word often abbreviates "maintaining family ties.".
Gentleness that chooses the least harmful effective way. It is wise and controlled gentleness, not weakness or refusal to correct.
Forbearing self-control when one has the power to retaliate. Without context, the same spelling can also mean a dream.
Deliberate composure that avoids rash action. It is thoughtful restraint, not laziness or indecision.
Dignified calm arising from seriousness and self-command. It is inward steadiness reflected outwardly, not stiffness or social status.
Honourable character and socially recognized decency that protect human dignity. Although often translated "manliness," the ethical quality is not limited to men.
Noble readiness to protect, assist, and act generously. It denotes moral courage and magnanimity, not aristocratic manners.
Swift assistance to someone in distress, especially when courage is needed. It includes initiative and solidarity, not emergency technique alone.
Ready and expansive giving without painful reluctance. It suggests an open-handed disposition, not merely the size of a gift.
Nobility expressed through generosity, honour, and gracious treatment. It is broader than hosting guests and can describe moral excellence.
Freedom from stinginess shown in willing expenditure. It emphasizes ease of giving rather than extravagance.
Putting one's wealth, effort, time, or status at the service of a worthy cause. It includes personal exertion and sacrifice, not money alone.
Sharing another person's burden through practical, material, and emotional support. It means standing with someone in hardship, not offering comforting words alone.
Faithfully completing promises, covenants, rights, and obligations. It concerns fulfilment and integrity, not allegiance regardless of truth.
Disciplined restraint from unlawful desire and degrading dependence. It includes sexual, financial, and verbal self-restraint.
Moral and physical courage governed by wisdom. Islamic ethics places it between cowardice and recklessness.
Aspirational energy directed toward noble aims. It is elevation of purpose, not status-seeking.
Serious, sustained exertion rather than play or negligence. It combines resolve and work; tone determines whether it contrasts with joking.
Steady continuation despite difficulty and delay. It stresses repeated disciplined effort, not stubborn attachment to error.
Outlasting opposition through greater steadfastness. It implies competing in endurance, not merely waiting.
Sustained vigilance and readiness in defence of duty. In Qur'anic and devotional usage, it may refer either to frontier service or disciplined spiritual watchfulness.
Mutual assistance in what is righteous and beneficial. Cooperation is praised or blamed according to the purpose it serves.
Communal mutual responsibility so that vulnerable members are not abandoned. It is an obligation-bearing social ethic, not sentiment alone.
Reciprocal active mercy among people. It stresses a community in which members give mercy to one another.
Emotionally recognizing and sharing another person's condition. Sermons usually connect this fellow feeling with practical support.
Disciplined and fitting conduct toward Allah, revelation, people, and particular situations. It combines knowledge, restraint, and propriety rather than etiquette alone.
Dignified modesty in appearance, speech, and social conduct. It denotes protected dignity rather than shame toward the body or ordinary interaction.
Gentle and accessible humility toward those under one's care. The expression is a Qur'anic image of tenderness, like a bird lowering its wing.
Purposeful restraint of speech when speaking would cause harm or bring no benefit. It does not justify withholding truth when testimony or intervention is required.
Guarding speech from falsehood, injury, and useless excess. It is a comprehensive discipline of verbal accountability.
Careful testing that separates sound information or character from what is defective. It includes purification through examination or trial, not fault-finding for its own sake.
Pausing long enough for judgment and action to mature. It is disciplined deliberation, not fear-driven indecision.
Concealing a person's non-public fault while encouraging correction and avoiding scandal. It does not justify hiding ongoing abuse, public danger, or violations of others' rights.
Courteous accommodation used to prevent harm while preserving principle. It differs from compromising truth merely to gain approval.
Wisely overlooking minor faults that one has noticed. It does not mean ignoring serious harm or neglecting responsibility.
Refraining from deserved personal retaliation despite having power. The expression praises moral strength, while public rights may still require justice.
Containing anger so it does not govern speech or action. It means mastery and redirection, not denial of emotion or tolerated abuse.
Restoring sound relations between estranged people. It is a major communal duty involving truth, justice, and reconciliation.
Warm, welcoming openness shown in the face and manner. It is socially beneficial graciousness, not forced happiness.
Meeting people with an open, pleasant, and approachable expression. It is a classical idiom and should not be translated literally as "a loose face.".
Giving urgent help to a person in acute distress. The expression conveys both urgency and moral responsibility.
Removing or easing another person's severe distress. The Prophetic expression connects relieving people in this life with receiving divine relief in the Hereafter.
Helping people meet legitimate and pressing needs. The word refers to needs and affairs, not every personal desire.
Supporting a dependent, burdened, or incapable person who cannot manage alone. It is a classical expression and does not mean carrying everyone physically.
Empowering and assisting those with limited power or capacity. It may be social, financial, physical, or situational; the phrase need not demean.
Supporting the wronged person in recovering safety and rights. It is effective advocacy and protection, not military victory.
Restoring wrongfully taken rights to their owners. It means violated rights or wrongful exactions, not abstract injustices.
Fulfilling the claims and obligations owed to Allah and to people. A right held by one person becomes a duty upon the person who owes it.
Honouring the persons, rights, times, places, and limits made inviolable by Allah. It is broader than respecting sacred objects.
Honouring the visible rites and symbols designated by Allah. It means reverent observance, not enlarging or idolizing symbols.
A heart free of rancour, envy, and malicious intent toward others. The expression is an idiom for inward moral soundness, not physical chest safety.
Inward clarity unclouded by persistent malice, vanity, or duplicity. It does not imply sinlessness; it describes cultivated moral lucidity.
Cleansing inward motives and states from spiritual corruption. It concerns intention and character, not ritual purification.
The recognized excellences of stable moral character. It points to embodied virtues rather than abstract moral theories.
The highest and most noble forms of moral character. It denotes elevated excellences, not generosity alone.
Gracious ease, generosity, and forbearance in lawful dealings. It does not mean unrestricted permissiveness or indifference to principle.
Making religious duties practicable through lawful ease and concession. It does not mean altering the religion simply to choose the least demanding option.
Removing excessive hardship recognized by Islamic law. Here, "haraj" means serious constriction, not social embarrassment.
Upright moderation that avoids blameworthy excess and neglect. It is guided by principle, not by automatically choosing the numerical midpoint.
Giving multiple legitimate claims their proportionate due. It is ethical integration, not mathematical equality.
A just, balanced, and morally excellent religious orientation. It does not mean compromise between truth and falsehood.
Regular continuation of a good act even when small. It stresses stable practice rather than unbroken action at every moment.
Sustainable and measured devotion without negligence or self-destructive excess. It expresses the Prophetic ideal of steady worship within human capacity.
Using available periods as opportunities for worship and benefit. It implies valuing a fleeting opportunity, not exploitation.
Ordering duties and benefits according to their real religious importance. It prevents lesser goods from displacing greater obligations.
The juristic method of weighing competing benefits and harms when they cannot all be achieved or avoided. It is more than ordinary compromise.
Seeking reputation by making one's good deeds heard or talked about. It is closely related to showing off, but often focuses on being praised through reports rather than direct observation.
Self-admiration that credits oneself and forgets divine grace. It is inward moral conceit, not healthy recognition of progress.
Actively refusing submission out of a claimed superiority. It implies enacted resistance, especially toward divine command.
Ostentatious self-importance displayed in bearing, dress, or conduct. It is pride made visible, not every confident appearance.
Deceptive confidence produced by false appearances, wishful thinking, or worldly attraction. It is being deluded, not merely admiring one's looks.
Wishing to receive a blessing similar to another person's without wanting their blessing removed. It is positive emulation, not envy.
Stored hostility that remains in the heart and seeks retaliation. It is sustained inward enmity, not a passing hurt.
Deep concealed rancour or treacherous resentment. It denotes hidden hostility that contaminates relationships.
Settled hatred and mutual aversion. It describes a relational condition that can be socially cultivated.
Hostility that fills the space between people and prolongs estrangement. It emphasizes charged interpersonal hostility, often blocking forgiveness.
A false accusation so serious that it leaves the accused stunned. It is stronger than an ordinary lie.
A grave fabricated falsehood that reverses or distorts reality. It is often used for calumny.
Knowingly stating or conveying what is contrary to reality. Its seriousness varies with intention, subject, and harm, but deliberate falsehood is the central meaning.
Deliberately distorted speech, testimony, or presentation that makes falsehood appear sound. It includes false testimony and deceptive appearance, not words alone.
Gross indecency or excess in speech and conduct. It is whatever crosses recognized moral bounds in an ugly way.
Habitually coarse, abusive, or shameless speech. It denotes verbal foulness that reflects degraded character.
Mutual or direct reviling and insulting. It is personal abuse, not merely using taboo words.
Invoking exclusion from Allah's mercy. It is a grave religious formula, not an ordinary insult.
Attacking another's honour, lineage, integrity, or standing. In moral discourse it is verbal or reputational assault.
Ridiculing a person in order to belittle them. It is contemptuous mockery, not all humour or joking.
Treating truth, religion, or people as objects of derisive scorn. It conveys contempt and can be doctrinally grave when directed at sacred matters.
Calling one another by offensive labels or nicknames. It highlights a culture of exchanged humiliation.
Conduct that violates the reverence or respect appropriate to a person, sacred matter, or situation. It is broader than poor etiquette.
Grave undutifulness and harmful conduct toward parents. It includes injury, contempt, and abandonment, not every disagreement.
Severing a relationship that one is religiously required to maintain. It most often concerns kinship but can also describe an unjustified social rupture.
Betraying a trust, covenant, confidence, or entrusted right. It is broader than betrayal of a state.
Violating a pledge after giving another party security or confidence. It emphasizes treacherous reversal after assurance.
Breaking a solemn promise or covenant after confirming it. It evokes unravelling something firmly twisted.
Denying a truth or favour that one inwardly recognizes. It implies culpable refusal, not simple lack of knowledge.
Denying or covering over gratitude for a blessing. Depending on context, the word can mean ingratitude and may also be connected with disbelief.
Arrogant exultation in blessings that leads to ingratitude and wrongdoing. It condemns corrupted enjoyment, not happiness itself.
Arrogant, heedless exuberance produced by prosperity. It describes morally intoxicated self-indulgence, not ordinary cheerfulness.
Exceeding proper limits in spending, consumption, behaviour, or even otherwise lawful activity. It is broader than wasting money.
Dissipating wealth into wrongful or useless uses. The wrongdoing concerns where resources are directed, not only the amount spent.
Possessive greed combining stinginess with an urge to acquire what others have. It is stronger than ordinary reluctance to spend.
Withholding what is due or appropriate despite having the ability to give. Unlike shuhh, the word focuses mainly on withholding rather than coveting.
Covetous desire for what another person possesses or controls. It is blameworthy when gain becomes more important than dignity, justice, or duty.
Intense eagerness to acquire or retain something. The word can praise diligence, but in moral warnings it often means grasping attachment.
Insatiable greed that is not satisfied by sufficiency. It stresses voracious excess rather than prudent desire.
A payment, gift, or benefit used to corrupt a duty or obtain an undeserved advantage. Its moral nature is determined by its purpose, not the label given to it.
Secretly misappropriating communal, entrusted, or public property. The term has a strong religious association with betrayal of public trust and war gains.
Illicit gain that morally corrupts or destroys the person who consumes it. It includes bribery, extortion, and other unlawful earnings.
Wrongfully taking, using, or benefiting from other people's wealth. "Eating" is a Qur'anic idiom for unjust appropriation.
Culpably delaying payment of a due debt despite ability. It is a specific financial injustice, not general delay.
Giving less than what is due in weight, measure, quality, or rights. The Qur'anic warning extends beyond marketplace scales to any unfair shortchanging.
Withholding needed goods in order to create harmful scarcity or manipulate prices. It is a specific juristic wrong and is not identical to every monopoly.
Deceiving another by concealing defects or presenting something falsely. It includes commercial, educational, relational, and religious deception.
Concealing a relevant defect or creating a misleading impression in a transaction or transmitted report. Its specific technical meaning depends on whether the context is law, commerce, or hadith.
Inducing a false belief through manipulation or concealed intent. It can describe interpersonal trickery or self-deception before Allah.
Secretly arranging an outcome through means the other party does not perceive. When attributed to Allah, it denotes His decisive response to wrongful plotting, not moral deceit.
Purposeful hidden strategizing to overcome or harm an opponent. It can be defensive or blameworthy depending on agent and context.
Crossing protected limits and violating another person's body, property, dignity, or rights. It is broader than physical aggression.
A culpable sin or moral burden that holds a person back from good. It can refer to the offence itself or the burden it creates.
A conspicuously grave indecency that exceeds moral limits. It often refers to sexual wrongdoing but is not limited to it.
Sins classified as less grave than major sins. They remain blameworthy and can become severe through persistence, contempt, or accumulation.
Sins that people dismiss as insignificant even though their accumulation can be destructive. The word criticizes the person's minimization of them.
Knowingly persisting in wrongdoing without repentance. Persistence can make repeatedly dismissed "small" sins morally grave.
Openly publicizing one's sin without shame, sometimes encouraging others to imitate it. It does not include admitting a fault privately in order to seek help or repent.

Displaying adornment or bodily attractions in a conspicuous way prohibited by Islamic modesty norms. The precise application depends on legal and social context and is not identical to ordinary grooming.

Seclusion between adults of opposite sexes who are legally marriageable to one another, in circumstances where normal public access or oversight is absent. It is a technical legal setting, not every form of privacy.
Sexual intercourse outside a valid marriage as defined by Islamic law. The term includes both adultery and fornication, while legal punishment requires an exceptionally high standard of proof.
Accusing a chaste person of unlawful sexual intercourse without the legally required proof. It is a specific major offence, not every form of defamation.
Any intoxicating substance that clouds the intellect, classically exemplified by wine. The legal meaning is based on intoxication, not the source ingredient alone.
Gambling or games of chance in which wealth is transferred through uncertain gain and loss. It does not include every competition or ordinary business risk.
Occult practice seeking extraordinary effects through prohibited means. The theological and legal category should not be automatically applied to stage illusion or entertainment tricks.
Claiming access to hidden information through spirits or occult intermediaries. In sermon language, it means soothsaying, not priesthood.
Claiming hidden knowledge through divination, signs, or alleged supernatural insight. It can include more than predicting future events.
Treating an omen as an independent cause for good or bad action. It is specifically omen-based pessimism that alters decisions.
The omen or superstitious foreboding itself. Its root arose from birds, but the concept covers many supposed signs.
Partisan loyalty that supports one's tribe or group even when it is unjust. The condemnation concerns loyalty overriding truth, not group identity itself.
A condition of ignorance, arrogance, and lawlessness opposed to divine guidance. It can describe recurring moral patterns, not only Arabia before Islam.
Corruption or disorder that damages moral, social, political, economic, or environmental life. It is broader than bribery.
Actively causing corruption or undermining what is sound. It stresses agency in spreading damage.
Brazen transgression that breaks through the restraints of righteousness. It evokes bursting beyond boundaries, often with shameless persistence.
Exceeding rightful limits through power, wealth, pride, or rebellion. It can describe people, societies, rulers, or even overflowing water.
Wrongful transgression, oppression, or pursuit of superiority. In legal and political contexts, it can also refer to rebellion, so the surrounding context matters.
Hardness of heart that blocks mercy, receptivity, and moral response. It is inward insensitivity, not firm enforcement of justice.
A Qur'anic image of rust or covering formed on the heart through accumulated sin. It describes loss of spiritual receptivity, not a physical substance.
A Qur'anic image of the heart becoming unreceptive after persistent rejection. It describes a consequence of culpable refusal, not literal printing.
A Qur'anic image of the heart being sealed against guidance after persistent rejection. It is a grave spiritual condition, not a medical description.
Spiritual hardness that makes reminders and suffering fail to awaken mercy. It is a cultivated moral state, not an immutable personality trait.
The heart's loss of spiritual awareness and responsiveness. A metaphor for moral-spiritual lifelessness, not bodily death.
Personal desire treated as an authority against truth and duty. The word does not condemn every desire, only desire followed in opposition to guidance.
Allowing appetites to direct conduct without lawful restraint. The criticism targets domination by desire, not human appetite itself.
Prolonged worldly expectation that delays repentance and useful action. It means living as though death and accountability were remote, not healthy hope.
Deliberately turning away from truth or reminder after it reaches a person. It is active disengagement, not simple distraction or lack of exposure.
Diversion that occupies a person away from what deserves greater priority. Its moral value depends on what it distracts from, not amusement alone.
Play or activity treated without ultimate seriousness. In sermons, it often describes the temporary nature of worldly life and does not make all recreation forbidden.
Acting or enduring hardship while consciously seeking reward from Allah. Intention transforms ordinary service or suffering into an act of worship.
The affliction that has befallen a person. It may be bereavement, illness, loss, or any tested hardship.
A harmful event that strikes a person or community by Allah's permission. It can mean loss, illness, or public calamity and does not by itself prove divine anger.
A test from Allah that reveals, educates, and distinguishes people's responses. It can occur through prosperity as well as adversity.
A test that reveals the reality of faith, character, or ability. In sermon language, it is a moral or existential examination rather than an academic test.
A severe ordeal that examines and exposes steadfastness. It implies prolonged pressure, including persecution.
A condition of constriction, hardship, or intensified difficulty. It can describe circumstances, not harsh character alone.
Adversity involving pain, harm, or material constriction. It is commonly paired with prosperity and ease.
Prosperity and ease that can themselves test gratitude and character. It describes favourable circumstances, not happiness alone.
Severe deprivation, poverty, or distress that presses upon life. It emphasizes material hardship.
A shaking that unsettles the earth, society, or a person's certainty. It may be literal, eschatological, or metaphorical for an extreme trial.
A state of compelling necessity in which ordinary choice is severely constrained. In Islamic law, it can change rulings but requires more than inconvenience.
A necessity whose absence threatens an essential interest such as life, religion, intellect, family, or property. It is a technical legal threshold, not every strong need.
A significant need whose neglect causes real hardship without reaching the level of dire necessity. Islamic law distinguishes it from both emergency and luxury.
Genuine difficulty or constriction that may trigger lawful facilitation. It concerns burden, not moral harshness.
Ease and practicability intended within obedience to Allah. It does not mean that religion requires no effort, sacrifice, or discipline.
Relief and opening granted by Allah after severe constriction. The phrase nurtures hope without guaranteeing a particular worldly result or timetable.
Hopeful confidence in Allah's wisdom, mercy, and fulfilment of His promise. It coexists with repentance and effort; it is not presumption of immunity from consequences.
Accepting Allah's decree without inward rebellion while continuing lawful action. It does not require liking pain, refusing treatment, or abandoning efforts at improvement.
Trustfully yielding one's judgment and will to established divine guidance. It is conscious submission, not unthinking passivity.
Using lawful practical causes and means while relying on Allah for the outcome. It rejects both fatalism and belief that causes operate independently of Him.
Neglecting effort while falsely claiming reliance on Allah. It is the blameworthy opposite or counterfeit of genuine reliance.
Actively resisting oppression, temptation, or destructive pressure. Its moral value depends on what is resisted and the methods used.
Sustained struggle to govern desire, anger, habit, and ego according to divine guidance. It is inner moral discipline, not violence against oneself.
Remaining purposeful and unbroken under sustained pressure. The word has modern political associations but also a wider meaning of resilient endurance.
Adapting permissible methods while preserving essential principles. It is not surrendering foundational beliefs or duties.
Gradual recovery after physical, emotional, communal, or spiritual harm. The word does not imply immediate or complete restoration.
An inward opening granted by Allah that produces receptivity, courage, and ease in carrying truth. It is a Qur'anic idiom, not a medical procedure.
